_note: The number archetypes' pages, one to six, as archetypes of order tied to the Self. The walk material (the position, its QL formulation and gloss, the number in von Franz) comes from curation/ql.json — one address for the QL, composed here, never copied. These sections carry Jung's own number material: the monad (CW9ii ¶340-341), the dyad (CW9ii ¶426, CW10 ¶806), the triad and its dilemma (CW12 ¶25, CW11 ¶183, CW9ii ¶234), the quaternity and the archetype of order (CW10 ¶803-805, CW9ii ¶381), the quintessence (CW10 ¶738, CW11 ¶160, CW8 ¶931), and the return with the Self (CW10 ¶805, CW9i pdf p424, CW12 ¶310). The egg block carries the three witnesses to one image: Pauli's dream with the site's count as six stages (QL, W § II — the 0/1 frame's start forgone, so the shape is visible and never named), Jung's CW9ii ¶345 footnote, and the pentadic mandala of CW9i ¶615. Quotations are placed by the corpus (scripts/numbers.mjs); nothing is typed. `stages` are the site's own count for the dream and are marked QL wherever they are shown.
line: Jung's statements on the numbers one to six (Aion, Psychology and Alchemy, Flying Saucers, the letters to Pauli), beside von Franz's Number and Time and the QL framework's six positions.

dream.quote: A woman comes with a bird, which lays a large egg.

footnote.quote: but the 'punctum solis' is apart from these four, in the midst of the yolk (which) is the chick.

To the scholiast of the "Tractatus aureus" it is the midpoint, the "circulus exiguus" and "mediator" which reconciles the hostile elements and "by persistent rotation changes the angular form of the square into a circular one like itself."
the starting point of creation.153 Similarly John Dee says that all things originated from the point and the monad.154 Indeed, God himself is simultaneously both the centre and the circumference.

mandala.quote: In the centre is the egg encircled by the snake; outside, apotropaic wings and eyes.
The mandala is exceptional in that it has a pentadic structure.

one.line: Jung on the One: the Monad of Monoïmos in Aion (CW9ii ¶340–341) and the number 1 in letter 63 to Pauli.

sections.title: The monad
sections.line: Aion (CW9ii ¶340–341, 1951): Hippolytus's report of the single Monad of Monoïmos, and Jung's comment on it.

quotes.quote: This Man is a single Monad, uncompounded [and] indivisible, [yet] compounded [and] divisible; loving and at peace with all things [yet] warring with all things and at war with itself in all things; unlike and like [itself], as it were a musical harmony containing all things
quotes.voice: Monoïmos, in Hippolytus, quoted by Jung

quotes.quote: This paradoxical idea of the Monad in Mono'imos describes the psychological nature of the self as conceived by a thinker of the second century under the influence of the Christian message.

sections.title: In the letter to Pauli
sections.line: Letter 63 (October 1953): the number 1; the scan of the letter is damaged in this sentence and the quotation is kept as the scan reads it.

quotes.quote: the One, absolute, nondivisible (advaita A two-less [Zweitlose]) and thus the unconscious, the beginning.

two.line: Jung on the two: the division of the One in letter 63 to Pauli, and the dyad and the self in Aion and Flying Saucers.

sections.title: The dyad
sections.line: Aion (CW9ii ¶426, 1951): the self as a union of conscious and unconscious; Flying Saucers (CW10 ¶806, 1958): the complexio oppositorum of Cusanus beside the dyad.

quotes.quote: Psychologically the self is a union of conscious (masculine) and unconscious (feminine). It stands for the psychic totality.

The symbols of the self coincide with the God-images, as, for instance, the complexio oppositorum of Cusanus with the dyad, or the definition of God as a "circle whose centre is everywhere and the circumference nowhere" with Angelucci’s sign of the hydrogen atom.
2 = the division of the One, the pair, the connection, the difference

three.line: Jung on the three: the Trinity and the missing fourth (CW12 ¶25, CW11 ¶183, CW9ii ¶237), three as a relative totality (CW9ii ¶351), and the number 3 in letter 63 to Pauli.

sections.title: The triad, and the dilemma
sections.line: CW12 ¶25: dogma and the uneven numbers; CW11 ¶183: the dilemma of three and four, from the opening of the Timaeus; CW9ii ¶237: the first coinciding with the fourth, in the axiom of Maria.

quotes.quote: dogma insists that three are one, while denying that four are one
the dilemma of three and four
the first coinciding with the fourth

sections.title: Three as a relative totality
sections.line: Aion (CW9ii ¶351, 1951): three as a relative totality, and three where the context indicates that it refers to the self.

quotes.quote: Three can be regarded as a relative totality, since it usually represents either a spiritual totality that is a product of thought, like the Trinity,8 or else an instinctual, chthonic one, like the triadic nature of the gods of the underworld—the "lower triad." Psychologically, however, three—if the context indicates that it refers to the self—should be understood as a defective quaternity or as a stepping-stone towards it.

sections.title: In the letter to Pauli
sections.line: Letter 63 (October 1953): the number 3; the scan is damaged where the line begins, and the quotation starts after the damage.

quotes.quote: the son, the first masculine number, etc.

four.line: Jung on four: the mandala's arithmetical structure and the number 4 (CW10 ¶803–805), the quaternity as an organizing schema (CW9ii ¶381), and the whole judgment (CW11 ¶246).

sections.title: The archetype of order
sections.line: Flying Saucers (CW10 ¶805, 1958): the mandala as a symbol of the self, whole numbers as archetypes of order, and the number 4, the Pythagorean tetraktys, named in particular.

quotes.quote: Psychologically, the rotundum or mandala is a symbol of the self.

The self is the archetype of order par excellence. The structure of the mandala is arithmetical, for “whole” numbers are likewise archetypes of order. This is true particularly of the number 4, the Pythagorean tetraktys.

sections.title: The viewfinder
sections.line: CW10 ¶803–804: the pattern of order compared to a viewfinder marked with a cross or a circle divided into four, and Jung's forty years of observing it in patients.

quotes.quote: The archetype thereby constellated represents a pattern of order which, like a psychological “viewfinder” marked with a cross or a circle divided into four, is superimposed on the psychic chaos so that each content falls into place and the weltering confusion is held together by the protective circle.

I have observed these phenomena in my patients for forty years and have come to the conclusion that this archetype is of central importance, or rather, that it gains in importance to the degree that the importance of the ego is lost.

sections.title: The organizing schema
sections.line: Aion (CW9ii ¶381): the quaternity called an organizing schema par excellence, compared to the crossed threads in a telescope.

quotes.quote: The quaternity is an organizing schema par excellence, something like the crossed threads in a telescope.

sections.title: The whole judgment
sections.line: A Psychological Approach to the Dogma of the Trinity (CW11 ¶246): the quaternity and the whole judgment, and the natural minimal division of the circle.

quotes.quote: The quaternity is an archetype of almost universal occurrence. It forms the logical basis for any whole judgment.
The ideal of completeness is the circle or sphere, but its natural minimal division is a quaternity.

five.line: Jung on five: the quinta essentia and the quincunx (CW10 ¶738, ¶774), and how rarely the pentad occurs in his work with patients (CW10 ¶775).

sections.title: The quinta essentia
sections.line: The quinta essentia in three passages: CW10 ¶738 (the circle divided into four with the centre), CW11 ¶160 (Johannes de Rupescissa's name for it) and CW8 ¶931 (Agrippa's spiritus mundi).

quotes.quote: This is a symbol of the quinta essentia, which is identical with the Philosophers’ Stone. It is the circle divided into four with the centre, or the divinity extended in four directions, or the four functions of consciousness with their unitary substrate, the self.
A famous alchemist, Johannes de Rupescissa (d. 1375),67 calls the quintessence “le ciel humain,” the human sky or heaven. For him it was a blue liquid and incorruptible like the sky.
By the spiritus mundi, the ligamentum animae et corporis, the quinta essentia,30 which he shares with the alchemists, Agrippa probably means what we would call the unconscious.

sections.title: The quincunx
sections.line: Flying Saucers (CW10 ¶774–775, 1958): the four forming a frame for the one, and how often the quaternity and the pentad turn up in Jung's practice.

quotes.quote: The fourth antithesis, unity and quaternity, appears united in the quincunx (Pls. III, IV), the four forming, as it were, a frame for the one, accentuated as the centre.
In my work with patients the quaternity symbol crops up very frequently, the pentad very rarely, and rather less rarely the triad.

six.line: Jung on the hexad and the number 6 (CW10 ¶771, CW9i ¶679) and on the self (CW10 ¶805, CW12 ¶310); von Franz on six in Number and Time.

sections.title: The hexad
sections.line: CW10 ¶771 (Flying Saucers, 1958) and CW9i ¶679 (Concerning Mandala Symbolism): the hexad as a totality symbol, and the number 6 in old tradition.

quotes.quote: The hexad is a totality symbol: 4 as the natural division of the circle, 2 as the vertical axis (zenith and nadir)—a spatial conception of totality.
According to old tradition the number 6 means creation and evolution, since it is a coniunctio of 2 and 3 (even and odd = female and male).

sections.title: The Self
sections.line: Jung on the self as the archetype of order par excellence (CW10 ¶805), the archetype of wholeness (CW9i, 1955) and the centre and the circumference (CW12 ¶310); none of the three passages names six.

quotes.quote: The self is the archetype of order par excellence. The structure of the mandala is arithmetical, for “whole” numbers are likewise archetypes of order. This is true particularly of the number 4, the Pythagorean tetraktys.

Indeed, it could even be called the archetype of wholeness. Because of this significance, the "quaternity of the One" is the schema for all images of God, as depicted in the visions of Ezekiel, Daniel, and Enoch, and as the representation of Horus with his four sons also shows.
The self is by definition the centre and the circumference of the conscious and unconscious systems.
